rows.verified: Dermatitis can result from skin contact with an irritant or from an allergic reaction.
Common visible signs include redness, scaling or flaking, blistering, weeping, cracking and swelling.
Irritant dermatitis can follow a single strong exposure or repeated contact with weaker irritants.
Repeated wet work, including frequent hand washing or prolonged wet hands, can contribute to irritant dermatitis.
Once a worker becomes sensitised to an allergen, subsequent skin contact can trigger allergic contact dermatitis.
HSE's APC approach is to Avoid contact where practical, Protect the skin and Check the skin regularly.
Suitable gloves, washing facilities, prompt removal of contamination and moisturising are listed as protective measures.
Regular skin checks can identify early signs and indicate whether exposure controls need reassessment.
Dermatitis risk depends on the substance, concentration, contact duration, wet work, glove choice, skin condition and control performance.
HSE dermatitis guidance is worker-, task-, substance-, exposure-, control- and time-specific and is not a parcel-level health probability.
HSE identifies lift trucks as particularly dangerous workplace vehicles.
Lift trucks are involved in about a quarter of workplace transport accidents on average.
Poor supervision and insufficient training are common contributors to lift-truck accidents.
Operators should receive training to the minimum standard in the Approved Code of Practice before operating covered lift trucks.
Rider-operated lift trucks include trucks controlled from seated and stand-on operating positions.
Guidance covers safe use, pedestrian protection, maintenance and thorough examination.
Lift-truck operators should be reassessed periodically and when new risks arise from changed working practices.
Workplace transport controls should separate people and vehicles and provide safe traffic routes where practical.
Lift-truck risk depends on truck type, load, site layout, pedestrian interaction, visibility, maintenance, supervision and operator competence.
HSE lift-truck evidence is vehicle-, site-, operator-, task-, control- and time-specific and is not a parcel-level collision probability.
Ladders should be used on firm, level and clean solid surfaces.
Ad-hoc packing such as bricks or blocks should not be used to level a ladder.
Work areas should be protected so ladders are not struck by vehicles or pushed over by doors and windows.
The public should be prevented from walking under or close to a ladder in use.
A ladder should preferably be tied at both stiles; a stability device or secure wedging are alternatives.
Footing a ladder is a last-resort securing method.
Access ladders should generally extend at least one metre above the landing point to provide a handhold.
Stepladders should not be used to access another level unless specifically designed for that purpose.
Ladder risk depends on surface, securing method, work duration, user competence, weather, traffic, public access and ladder condition.
HSE ladder guidance is equipment-, user-, site-, task-, weather-, control- and time-specific and is not a parcel-level fall probability.
